# Appendix A: Perturbation Targets for LOMM Recovery

Appendix A explains why the same block-measured linear panel gives different recovery margins for DynEGA, GraphicalVAR, and GIMME. The appendix separates a population structural matrix, estimation and graph-conversion error conditional on a usable fit, the community-detection map, and fit usability. Community detection is not part of an additive edge-error matrix, and a failed fit has no estimated graph.

Each pipeline is a composition

$$
\widehat{S}^{(r)}
\;\xrightarrow{\Pi_r}\;
\widetilde{W}^{(r)}
\;\xrightarrow{\mathcal{C}_r}\;
\widehat{\mathcal{B}}^{(r)},
$$

where $\widehat{S}^{(r)}$ is the fitted method-specific structure, $\Pi_r$ is the method-specific graph conversion, $\widetilde{W}^{(r)}$ is the graph supplied to community detection, $\mathcal{C}_r$ is the community algorithm, and $\widehat{\mathcal{B}}^{(r)}$ is the returned partition. Let $U_r$ denote the event that a usable graph exists. Conditional on $U_r=1$,

$$
\widetilde{W}^{(r)}
=
W_*^{(r)}+E^{(r)},
$$

where $W_*^{(r)}$ is the population structural matrix induced by the method readout and $E^{(r)}$ collects finite-sample variation, derivative or model estimation, regularization, extraction, dependence-induced variance inflation, and systematic deviation of the realized population graph from the symmetric target. Community detection and fit failure are not part of $E^{(r)}$: the community algorithm acts after the graph is formed, and when $U_r=0$ there is no estimated graph to perturb.

The argument has three claims. First, idealized DynEGA and GraphicalVAR population graphs preserve the generating block support exactly under the symmetric linear block target, conditional on zero pooled cross-block moments after the relevant filtering or projection. Second, under the same target their within-block partial-correlation edges share one ceiling; where each edge sits below that ceiling is set by the method-specific filtered or projected signal-to-noise ratio, whose ordering is not determined by the block algebra. Third, GIMME has a different mathematical status because recovery depends on path search, convergence, extraction, averaging, graph conversion, and completion. The sections below define the target, derive the two population graph maps, state the perturbation margin, and summarize the method comparison.

| Result or layer | Main assumptions | Planned departures and interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| Exact block support | Zero pooled cross-block moments after filtering or projection (sufficient: independent zero-conditional-mean latent factors), one primary loading per indicator, and independent measurement errors | Cross-loadings, correlated residuals, and correlated shocks test how cross-block edges erode separation |
| Per-channel filter invariance | The same linear temporal filter is applied to every indicator, with boundary handling fixed | Short records, embedding selection, and gate transitions can change finite-sample filter behavior |
| Within-block edge formula | Exchangeable loadings and error variances within a block, with positive filtered signal variance | Loading and variance jitter perturb edge equality while preserving the ideal support target |
| Connected-component recovery | The weakest population within-block edge exceeds the total graph perturbation conditional on a usable fit | Regularization, sampling error, and estimation contribute to the edge perturbation; fit failure removes the graph, and community detection acts after it |
| GIMME recovery decomposition | A usable contemporaneous graph can be extracted and partitioned | Convergence, timeout, extraction, symmetrization, and completion are separate stages of the pipeline readout |

: Assumptions behind the Appendix A population results and the prespecified revision challenges. {#tbl-lomm-assumptions}

## A.1 Linear Block Target and Pooled Moments

In this appendix, $Y_j$ corresponds to a main-text pre-link score channel $z_j$, $X_f$ to the ungated latent level $x_f$, and $Z_f=a_fX_f$ to the activity-scaled latent level $\tilde{x}_f$. The appendix drops video indices and loading and variance jitter to define a symmetric population target.

Consider a population LOMM with $m$ latent dimensions, $k$ observed indicators per dimension, and $p=mk$ observed score channels. Let $B_1,\ldots,B_m$ denote the true indicator blocks. For indicator $j \in B_f$, use the equal-loading, equal-error measurement model

$$
Y_j(t)=\lambda Z_f(t)+\varepsilon_j(t),
\qquad
Z_f(t)=a_f(t)X_f(t),
$$

where $Z_f(t)$ is the activity-scaled latent oscillator for dimension $f$, $\lambda>0$, and $\varepsilon_j(t)$ is measurement error with variance $\psi=s_\varepsilon^2$. Measurement errors are independent across indicators and time in this target, so $\operatorname{Cov}(\varepsilon_j(t),\varepsilon_\ell(s))=0$ whenever $j\neq \ell$ or $t\neq s$.

Population moments are taken over a common retained analysis window $\mathcal{R}$ of video--time rows shared by every pipeline. For any quantity $g$,

$$
\langle g\rangle_{\mathcal R}
=
\frac{1}{|\mathcal R|}
\sum_{(i,t)\in\mathcal R}
E(g_{it}),
$$

and, for any filtered process $U$,

$$
\operatorname{Var}_{\mathcal R}(U)
=
\left\langle
\{U-\langle U\rangle_{\mathcal R}\}^{2}
\right\rangle_{\mathcal R}.
$$

All variances and covariances in this appendix are time-averaged centered second moments over the common analysis window $\mathcal{R}$.

Exact block support is imposed through zero pooled cross-block moments over the retained rows. For every pair $f\neq g$ and every method-relevant filter or projection, the corresponding centered cross-block covariance is assumed to be zero. A sufficient condition is that the oscillator states are independent across factors at all relevant times, have zero conditional mean at every retained row, the activity schedules are deterministic or independent of the states and shocks, and dynamic shocks are independent across factors. Uncoupled dynamic equations alone do not imply zero pooled cross-block covariance.

Coordinated activity schedules do not by themselves create cross-block covariance when the factor states have zero conditional means. A shared deterministic initialization can create common mean transients and violate the pooled zero-cross-covariance condition even when the dynamic equations and shocks are uncoupled. The checked-in common start is therefore a structured departure from the ideal target, while the revised independent zero-mean starts are designed to remove this channel.

Activity gating makes $Z_f$ nonstationary by design, which is why the covariances in this appendix are defined as pooled centered moments rather than as stationary second moments. Loading jitter, item-level variance jitter, switching schedules, initialization transients, finite-sample activity imbalance, and estimator behavior are treated as departures or perturbations around this symmetric target.

## A.2 Filtered Panels and Two Graph Readouts

The derivation uses two population graph maps for a per-channel filtered block panel. DynEGA estimates local derivatives of every channel, and a lag difference is a simple analytic example of the same channelwise operation. GraphicalVAR is handled separately in A.3 because its lag-1 projection residuals come from a multivariate projection rather than from an identical filter applied to each channel.

Let $L$ denote a fixed per-channel linear filter with coefficients $\ell_0,\ldots,\ell_q$, identical boundary handling for every channel, and no window crossing a video boundary. Applying $L$ to the measurement model for $j \in B_f$ gives

$$
(LY_j)(t)=\lambda\,(LZ_f)(t)+(L\varepsilon_j)(t),
$$

so the filtered panel keeps the one-factor block structure. Write

$$
V_{L,f}=\operatorname{Var}_{\mathcal R}(LZ_f),
\qquad
\psi_L=\operatorname{Var}_{\mathcal R}(L\varepsilon_j)
$$

for the filtered common-signal variance and the filtered noise variance, both centered over the common analysis window. For iid base measurement error,

$$
\psi_L
=
\psi\sum_{r=0}^{q}\ell_r^2,
$$

and overlapping windows induce the lag covariance

$$
\operatorname{Cov}\{(L\varepsilon_j)_t,(L\varepsilon_j)_{t+h}\}
=
\psi\sum_r\ell_r\ell_{r-h}.
$$

Filtering preserves cross-channel error independence under the ideal error model, so the contemporaneous same-row block covariance remains diagonal plus rank one. Overlapping windows generally make filtered errors serially correlated. This serial dependence does not change the ideal same-row block covariance, but it changes effective sample size, regularization behavior, and sampling variability; it is therefore treated as an estimation issue in A.4 rather than absorbed silently into the population object.

Write $J_k=\mathbf{1}_k\mathbf{1}_k^\top$. The within-block covariance matrix of the filtered channels is

$$
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{L,f}
=
\lambda^{2}V_{L,f}\,J_k+\psi_L I_k,
\qquad
\theta_{L,f}=\frac{\lambda^{2}V_{L,f}}{\psi_L},
$$

provided the cross-block filtered moments vanish. Define

$$
C_{L,fg}
=
\left\langle
\{LZ_f-\mu_{L,f}\}
\{LZ_g-\mu_{L,g}\}
\right\rangle_{\mathcal R},
\qquad
\mu_{L,f}
=
\langle LZ_f\rangle_{\mathcal R}.
$$

The block-diagonal covariance and precision formulas in this section require $C_{L,fg}=0$ for all $f\neq g$: exact block support is conditional on these zero pooled cross-block moments after filtering. The filtered signal-to-noise ratio $\theta_{L,f}$ is the only quantity through which the filter enters the population graph.

The filtered panel admits two graph readouts. The marginal readout uses correlations directly. For two distinct indicators $j,\ell \in B_f$,

$$
w^{M}_f(L)
=
\left|\operatorname{Cor}(LY_j,LY_\ell)\right|
=
\frac{\theta_{L,f}}{1+\theta_{L,f}}.
$$

The partial readout conditions each pair on all other retained observed channels; under exact block diagonality, the other blocks do not change the within-block calculation. Using the Sherman-Morrison identity,

$$
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{L,f}^{-1}
=
\psi_L^{-1}
\left[
I_k-
\frac{\theta_{L,f}}{1+k\theta_{L,f}}
J_k
\right],
$$

and the absolute partial correlation between two indicators in the same block is

$$
w^{P}_f(L)
=
\frac{\theta_{L,f}}{1+(k-1)\theta_{L,f}}.
$$

Because activity gating makes the row distribution time-varying, the inverse of the pooled covariance is used here as an algebraic partial-correlation readout. It is not interpreted as the conditional-independence graph of one stationary Gaussian process. Under the zero cross-block moment condition, the filtered precision matrix is block-diagonal and cross-block partial correlations are exactly zero. These marginal and partial readouts therefore preserve the generating block support without error for the per-channel filtered population object, and the population graph has block-clique form for any per-channel filter,

$$
\mathbf{W}_*
=
\operatorname{blockdiag}
\left(
w_1(J_k-I_k),\ldots,w_m(J_k-I_k)
\right),
\qquad
w_f\in\{w^{M}_f(L),\,w^{P}_f(L)\}.
$$

The two readouts differ in how much within-block signal they keep. For the same signal-to-noise ratio $\theta$,

$$
\frac{w^P(\theta)}{w^M(\theta)}
=
\frac{1+\theta}{1+(k-1)\theta},
$$

so $w^P(\theta)<w^M(\theta)$ whenever $k>2$ and $\theta>0$. As $\theta \to \infty$,

$$
w^P(\theta)\to \frac{1}{k-1},
\qquad
w^M(\theta)\to 1.
$$

Under the equal-loading, equal-error symmetric population target, the partial readout compresses an arbitrarily strong common-source signal toward a ceiling set by block size alone: with four indicators per dimension, no within-block partial-correlation edge can exceed $1/3$ under that symmetric target. Both readout maps are increasing in $\theta$, so filter and readout separate cleanly. The filter sets $\theta_{L,f}$, and the readout maps $\theta_{L,f}$ to the edge weight supplied to community detection.

@fig-readout-curves compares the marginal and partial maps for the matched grid's four indicators per dimension. The marginal map is a pre-conditioning benchmark; neither implemented pipeline uses it. The vertical gap between the curves shows how much compression the partial map applies to the common-source signal. The shaded band marks the $\lambda^2/s_\varepsilon^2$ span of the matched measurement grid, so the simulated loading and error conditions place $\theta_{L,f}$ inside the band up to the filtered common-signal variance $V_{L,f}$. Across that span, the marginal curve rises from mid-range values toward 1. The partial curve is already near its $1/3$ ceiling under the symmetric target: strong measurement conditions widen the common-source signal margin but cannot widen the partial-correlation edge beyond that symmetric-target ceiling.

```{r}
#| label: fig-readout-curves
#| fig-cap: "Population within-block edge weight as a function of the filtered signal-to-noise ratio for the marginal and partial readouts with four indicators per dimension under the equal-loading, equal-error symmetric population target. The dotted line marks the partial-readout ceiling $1/(k-1)=1/3$ under that symmetric target. The shaded band spans the loading-to-error-variance ratios of the matched simulation grid; the filtered common-signal variance multiplies the signal-to-noise ratio within this band. Higher edge weight means more within-block signal margin before estimation perturbations."
#| fig-align: center
#| out-width: "0.9\\linewidth"
#| fig-pos: "H"

readout_curves_path <- file.path("figures", "perturbation_readout_curves.pdf")
if (!file.exists(readout_curves_path)) {
  readout_curves_path <- file.path("paper", "figures", "perturbation_readout_curves.pdf")
}
knitr::include_graphics(readout_curves_path)
```

## A.3 Method-Specific Filters and Signal-to-Noise Ratios

The implemented pipelines are specific readout combinations. DynEGA estimates generalized local linear approximation (GLLA) derivatives of each score channel over a time-delay embedding window and then estimates a regularized partial-correlation network (EBICglasso) on the derivative panel. The implementation uses one observation interval as the GLLA `delta` and retains the generator's physical $dt=0.4$ in separate horizon metadata. Conversion to physical-time derivatives applies the same positive scale factor to every channel and therefore leaves the derivative correlation readout unchanged.

### A.3.1 DynEGA and a fixed derivative filter

For a fixed selected GLLA derivative filter with coefficient vector $\boldsymbol{\ell}$, let $R_{Z,f}$ denote the covariance matrix of the latent values entering the embedding window, centered over the common analysis window. Under iid white measurement error, the population filtered signal-to-noise ratio is

$$
\theta_{\mathrm{GLLA},f}
=
\frac{
\lambda^2\boldsymbol{\ell}^\top R_{Z,f}\boldsymbol{\ell}
}{
\psi\,\boldsymbol{\ell}^\top\boldsymbol{\ell}
}.
$$

This population expression is conditional on the chosen embedding and boundary rule; embedding selection and regularized estimation belong to the fitted pipeline. DynEGA's population graph is the partial readout evaluated at this ratio, $w_f^{P}(\theta_{\mathrm{GLLA},f})$.

A lag-$h$ difference, $\Delta_hY_j(t)=Y_j(t+h)-Y_j(t)$, gives a transparent analytic stand-in for that filter, with

$$
\theta_{f}^{\Delta_h}
=
\frac{
\lambda^2\operatorname{Var}_{\mathcal R}
\{Z_f(t+h)-Z_f(t)\}
}{
2\psi
},
$$

because independent measurement errors contribute $2\psi$ to the variance of every differenced channel. Both the lag difference and GLLA derivative estimation operate channel by channel. GLLA can reduce white measurement-noise variance by averaging over an embedding window, but it can also attenuate latent change components. Its signal-to-noise ratio is therefore scenario and embedding dependent.

### A.3.2 GraphicalVAR lag-1 projection

GraphicalVAR reads partial correlations from the residual covariance of a lag-1 vector autoregression. Its population object is defined here by a population unpenalized lag-1 linear projection, $\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{VAR}}$, rather than by a per-channel filter. For one symmetric block, define centered common-window lag-pair moments

$$
V_{-,f}=E_{\mathcal R}\{Z_f(t-1)^2\},
\qquad
V_{+,f}=E_{\mathcal R}\{Z_f(t)^2\},
\qquad
C_f=E_{\mathcal R}\{Z_f(t)Z_f(t-1)\},
$$

where the expectations are over retained within-video lag pairs after the same centering rule used by the estimator, and no lag pair crosses a clip boundary. Under equal loadings, equal serially independent measurement-error variances, zero cross-block lag-0 and lag-1 moments, and a population unpenalized lag-1 linear projection, the block moment matrices are

$$
S_{--,f}
=
\lambda^2V_{-,f}J_k+\psi I_k,
\qquad
S_{+-,f}
=
\lambda^2C_fJ_k,
\qquad
S_{++,f}
=
\lambda^2V_{+,f}J_k+\psi I_k.
$$

The population lag-1 coefficient matrix is

$$
B_f
=
S_{+-,f}S_{--,f}^{-1}
=
\frac{\lambda^2C_f}
{\psi+k\lambda^2V_{-,f}}
J_k.
$$

The lag-1 projection residual covariance is

$$
\Omega_{\mathrm{VAR},f}
=
S_{++,f}
-
S_{+-,f}S_{--,f}^{-1}S_{-+,f}
=
\psi I_k+c_{\mathrm{VAR},f}J_k,
\qquad
c_{\mathrm{VAR},f}
=
\lambda^2V_{+,f}
-
\frac{
k\lambda^4C_f^2
}{
\psi+k\lambda^2V_{-,f}
}.
$$

With

$$
\theta_{\mathrm{VAR},f}
=
\frac{c_{\mathrm{VAR},f}}{\psi},
$$

the residual covariance retains the diagonal-plus-rank-one form, and the compression map of A.2 applies at the residual scale:

$$
w_{\mathrm{VAR},f}^{P}
=
\frac{
\theta_{\mathrm{VAR},f}
}{
1+(k-1)\theta_{\mathrm{VAR},f}
}.
$$

This result defines the pooled lag-1 linear-projection residual covariance. Calling it an innovation covariance requires the stronger interpretation that the fitted lag-1 VAR supplies the relevant innovation process. Oscillator position need not be VAR(1), so the residuals can remain serially correlated. The block result requires zero cross-block lag-0 and lag-1 moments. It does not hold generally with cross-loadings, correlated factors, correlated errors, heterogeneous serial measurement error, cross-video lag construction, or incompatible centering.

### A.3.3 Stationary special case and claim boundary

For a stationary special case with

$$
V_{+,f}=V_{-,f}=V_f,
\qquad
C_f=\rho_{1,f}V_f,
\qquad
\theta_f=\frac{\lambda^2V_f}{\psi},
$$

the lag-1 residual ratio reduces to

$$
\theta_{\mathrm{VAR},f}
=
\theta_f
\left[
1-
\rho_{1,f}^2
\frac{k\theta_f}{1+k\theta_f}
\right],
$$

while a lag-1 difference gives

$$
\theta_{\Delta_1,f}
=
\theta_f(1-\rho_{1,f}).
$$

For $0<\rho_{1,f}<1$, $\theta_{\mathrm{VAR},f}>\theta_{\Delta_1,f}$. Therefore a simple first difference does not justify the claim that a derivative readout has higher signal-to-noise than the lag-1 residual readout. The regime limits are instructive: as $\rho_{1,f}\to1$,

$$
\theta_{\mathrm{VAR},f}
\to
\frac{\theta_f}{1+k\theta_f},
$$

and, if $\theta_f\to\infty$ in that limit,

$$
w_{\mathrm{VAR},f}^{P}
\to
\frac{1}{2k-1},
$$

whereas for fixed $\rho_{1,f}<1$ and $\theta_f\to\infty$ the within-block edge instead approaches the shared $1/(k-1)$ ceiling under the symmetric target.

The population comparison between DynEGA and GraphicalVAR then has a precise but limited form. Both population readouts supply partial-correlation edges to community detection, so under the equal-loading, equal-error symmetric population target both within-block edges are capped at $1/(k-1)$ and the generating block support is preserved in both population graphs, conditional on the zero cross-block moments stated above. The block algebra does not determine a general ordering between $\theta_{\mathrm{GLLA},f}$ and $\theta_{\mathrm{VAR},f}$. In the strongly autocorrelated regimes studied here, a larger GLLA signal-to-noise ratio is a design-specific expectation only if embedding-window noise averaging more than offsets attenuation of the latent derivative signal. This expectation must be tested from oracle or realized filtered covariances rather than assumed from the population block form. The remaining differences are pipeline perturbations, which A.4 collects in a single margin.

## A.4 Shared Perturbation Margin

Let a method's population graph have block-clique form

$$
\mathbf{W}_*^{(r)}
=
\operatorname{blockdiag}
\left(
w_1^{(r)}(J_k-I_k),\ldots,w_m^{(r)}(J_k-I_k)
\right),
$$

where edge weights are on the nonnegative scale supplied to community detection and all $m$ blocks share the same size $k$. For DynEGA and GraphicalVAR, $w_f^{(r)}$ equals $w_f^{P}(\theta_{\mathrm{GLLA},f})$ or $w_f^{P}(\theta_{\mathrm{VAR},f})$ from A.3, evaluated on the common analysis window. Conditional on $U_r=1$, define the perturbation after method-specific graph conversion as

$$
\delta_r
=
\|
\widetilde W^{(r)}
-
W_*^{(r)}
\|_{\max}
=
\max_{j\neq \ell}
\left|
\widetilde{W}^{(r)}_{j\ell}-W^{(r)}_{*,j\ell}
\right|.
$$

For any node $j \in B_f$, the estimated total connection to its true block is at least

$$
(k-1)(w_f^{(r)}-\delta_r),
$$

whereas its estimated total connection to any wrong block is at most

$$
k\delta_r.
$$

Thus each node has stronger total connection to its true block than to any wrong block whenever

$$
(k-1)(w_{\min}^{(r)}-\delta_r)>k\delta_r,
$$

or equivalently

$$
\delta_r
<
\frac{k-1}{2k-1}w_{\min}^{(r)}.
$$

For the matched grid with $k=4$, the sufficient node-level block-preference and threshold-separation condition is

$$
\delta_r < \frac{3}{7}w_{\min}^{(r)},
$$

conditional on a usable graph and on the exact block-support population target. This margin is not a guarantee that Louvain, Leiden, or Walktrap recover the blocks, because exact recovery depends on the implemented community-detection algorithm. The bound has a narrower consequence. Because $\tfrac{k-1}{2k-1}<\tfrac{1}{2}$, the condition forces every estimated cross-block edge below every estimated within-block edge, so any threshold $\tau\in(\delta_r,\,w_{\min}^{(r)}-\delta_r)$ deletes all cross-block edges, keeps each block a connected clique, and reproduces the generating blocks exactly as the connected components of the thresholded graph. Threshold separation alone needs only $\delta_r<w_{\min}^{(r)}/2$.

The margin treats perturbation as symmetric noise on every edge, which makes $\delta_r$ a worst-case envelope. Regularized estimation acts asymmetrically: glasso shrinkage lowers within-block edges, which reduces $w_{\min}^{(r)}$, and sets weak cross-block edges to zero, which supports block separation.

Under the equal-loading, equal-error symmetric population target, the two population partial-readout pipelines share the same ceiling. DynEGA and GraphicalVAR supply partial-correlation edges to community detection, so under that symmetric target $w_{\min}^{(r)}\leq 1/(k-1)$ for both pipelines, and with $k=4$ the sufficient perturbation margin approaches at most

$$
\delta_r
<
\frac{3}{7}\cdot\frac{1}{3}
=
\frac{1}{7}
$$

in the high-signal limit of the symmetric target. The population comparison therefore reduces to the two quantities identified in A.3: how close each filtered or projected signal-to-noise ratio keeps $w_{\min}^{(r)}$ to the shared ceiling, and how large each pipeline's realized perturbation $\delta_r$ is. The observed ordering does not identify which method has the larger population signal-to-noise ratio because estimation, regularization, graph conversion, and feasibility differ between pipelines. The full graphical vector-autoregression fit also adds larger estimation and timeout perturbations.

The margin also identifies which blocks are fragile in each scenario family. Activity gating enters the filtered signal directly: $V_{L,f}$ is the time-averaged centered variance of the filtered activity-scaled process over the common analysis window, so a dimension held at background gain contributes a small $\theta_{L,f}$ and a weak within-block edge. All $V_{L,f}$, $w_{\min}^{(r)}$, and $W_*^{(r)}$ are conditional on the common analysis window; this conditioning is essential for anti-damped factors, whose moments grow across the window. In the single-dominance families, background dimensions run at gains of 0.05--0.08 against active gains of 0.35--1.25 (Appendix E). Under comparable ungated filtered variances and error levels, background gains are expected to reduce $\theta_{L,f}$ and often determine the weakest block. The actual weakest block is the factor with the smallest scenario-specific $V_{L,f}$ and must be identified from the generated panel or population calculation; in the low-expression family every dimension sits near background activity. The margin therefore predicts the scenario-family ordering observed in @fig-dimension-recovery for DynEGA and GraphicalVAR: recovery is hardest where the activity schedule holds the weakest block's signal lowest. For GIMME, the same activity envelope is an expected stressor, but its effect is mediated by path search, convergence, extraction, averaging, graph conversion, and completion.

## A.5 GIMME as an Indirect Graph-Conversion Readout

The implemented GIMME comparator has a different mathematical status. Let $R_i^G$ denote the standardized residual covariance matrix extracted from `fit$psi` for usable clip $i$, and let $V_u$ be the number of usable clip matrices. The averaged matrix is

$$
\bar R_G
=
\frac{1}{V_u}
\sum_{i:U_i=1}R_i^G,
$$

taken over usable clips only, and the graph supplied to community detection is

$$
W_G
=
\left[
\operatorname{offdiag}
\left\{
\frac{\bar R_G+\bar R_G^\top}{2}
\right\}
\right]_+.
$$

This is a positive residual-correlation graph conversion, not a path graph and not a partial-correlation graph. The readout depends on path search, clip-level model selection, convergence, extraction, averaging, and graph conversion. We therefore summarize GIMME as an indirect graph-conversion pipeline without a closed-form block edge $w_f^G$.

Status-inclusive recovery also includes completion. For any pipeline, let $U$ denote the event that a usable fitted graph exists and $H$ the event that the returned partition is correct, conditional on usability. The status-inclusive hit event is

$$
H^*=U\cap H,
\qquad
P(H^*)
=
P(U)\,P(H\mid U).
$$

Failures and timeouts count as non-hits in $P(H^*)$, but they do not enter $P(H\mid U)$, and the structure-fit and repeated community-readout denominators are reported separately. The reported feasibility tables make this decomposition concrete. DynEGA returned usable graphs for every broad-grid and matched-grid row, so its status-inclusive and conditional hit rates coincide at 95.3%. GraphicalVAR completed 20,872 of 21,600 matched-grid structure fits (62,616 of 64,800 readout rows), so its 80.3% status-inclusive hit rate corresponds to a conditional hit rate of about 83% among usable readouts. GIMME completed 15,294 of 21,600 structure fits (45,882 of 64,800 readout rows), so its 25.9% status-inclusive hit rate corresponds to a conditional hit rate of about 37%. The decomposition separates GIMME's two losses: many fits return no usable graph, and partition quality after a usable graph remains well below the other pipelines.

## A.6 Method-Comparison Summary

```{r}
#| label: tbl-appendix-perturbation-summary
#| results: asis

perturbation_summary <- tibble::tribble(
  ~Pipeline, ~`Population signal`, ~`Main perturbation`, ~`Expected implication`,

  "GraphicalVAR", "$w_f^P(\\theta_{\\mathrm{VAR},f})$: partial readout of lag-1 projection residuals", "VAR estimation, regularization, lag-1 projection attenuation, timeouts", "Under the stated symmetric moment assumptions, the lag-1 projection residual covariance preserves block support and follows the same partial-correlation compression map; its signal-to-noise ratio is given by the A.3 formula",
  "GIMME", "No closed-form block signal for the implemented readout", "Path search, clip-level fitting, extraction, averaging, timeouts", "Recovery combines fit usability with a documented method-specific residual-covariance or path-matrix graph conversion"
)

print(knitr::kable(

))
```

# Appendix E: Supplementary Scenario Parameter Values

The final scenario families use the numeric settings below. The reported final runs fix the quality scale at $Q=0.75$. The base $\sigma_q$ vectors in the numeric dynamic-vector table are therefore the final-run innovation vectors, applied as per-step shock standard deviations at the step size used for each series length ($dt=0.4$ for 100-point series and $dt=0.25$ for 300-point series). The simulation code also supports configurable reruns with $\sigma_q=\text{scenario base }\sigma_q\times(Q/0.75)$.

Codes A--D use asymptotically stable template feedback. Codes E--F use ranked feedback with $\eta_f<0$ and $\zeta_f>0$, which produces finite-horizon anti-damped oscillations. Their interpretation is restricted to the reported observation horizons. The prospective empirical realism calibration compares unconstrained and stable negative-$\zeta$ grids; it does not alter these checked-in scenario parameters.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-scenario-schedule-supplement
#| results: asis

fmt_vec <- function(x) paste(sprintf("%.2f", x), collapse = "; ")
dimensions <- 2:4
template_eta <- c(-0.30, -0.55, -0.85, -1.10)
template_zeta <- c(-1.70, -1.00, -0.65, -0.30)
template_sigma <- c(0.12, 0.30, 0.45, 0.65)
ranked_eta <- -0.05 * seq_len(4)
ranked_zeta <- 0.06 + 0.02 * seq_len(4)

scenario_schedule_table <- tibble::tribble(
  ~Code, ~Family, ~Source, ~Switching, ~Gain, ~Dwell, ~`Feedback source`,
  "A", "Low-expression single dominance", "Generic", "No", "0.35 / 0.05", "1.00 / 1.00", "Template",
  "B", "High-expression single dominance", "Generic", "No", "1.00 / 0.08", "1.00 / 1.00", "Template",
  "C", "High-expression switching", "Generic", "Yes", "1.00 / 0.08", "0.20 / 0.45", "Template",
  "D", "High-expression rapid switching", "Generic", "Yes", "1.25 / 0.08", "0.03 / 0.10", "Template",
  "E", "Ranked-persistence", "Calibration-inspired", "No", "1.00 / 0.08", "1.00 / 1.00", "Ranked",
  "F", "Broad switching-geometry", "Calibration-inspired", "Yes", "1.10 / 0.10", "0.12 / 0.30", "Ranked"
)

make_dynamic_rows <- function(code, eta, zeta, sigma_base) {
  do.call(rbind, lapply(dimensions, function(dimension) {
    data.frame(
      Code = code,
      Dimensions = paste0(dimension, "D"),
      eta = fmt_vec(eta[seq_len(dimension)]),
      zeta = fmt_vec(zeta[seq_len(dimension)]),
      `Base sigma-q` = fmt_vec(sigma_base[seq_len(dimension)]),
      check.names = FALSE
    )
  }))
}

scenario_dynamic_table <- do.call(rbind, list(
  make_dynamic_rows("A", template_eta, template_zeta, template_sigma * 0.50),
  make_dynamic_rows("B", template_eta, template_zeta, template_sigma),
  make_dynamic_rows("C", template_eta, template_zeta, template_sigma),
  make_dynamic_rows("D", template_eta, template_zeta, template_sigma * 1.25),
  make_dynamic_rows("E", ranked_eta, ranked_zeta, rep(0.25, 4)),
  make_dynamic_rows("F", ranked_eta, ranked_zeta, rep(0.35, 4))
))

cat("\\begingroup\\scriptsize\\setlength{\\tabcolsep}{3pt}\n")
print(knitr::kable(
  scenario_schedule_table,
  format = "latex",
  longtable = TRUE,
  caption = "Scenario schedule and feedback-source settings for the final simulation families.",
  booktabs = TRUE,
  escape = FALSE,
  align = c("c", "p{1.75in}", "p{0.85in}", "c", "c", "c", "p{0.75in}")
))
cat("\\endgroup\n\n")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-scenario-stability-supplement
#| results: asis

scenario_vectors <- list(
  A = list(eta = template_eta, zeta = template_zeta),
  B = list(eta = template_eta, zeta = template_zeta),
  C = list(eta = template_eta, zeta = template_zeta),
  D = list(eta = template_eta, zeta = template_zeta),
  E = list(eta = ranked_eta, zeta = ranked_zeta),
  F = list(eta = ranked_eta, zeta = ranked_zeta)
)

stability_rows <- list()
stability_row <- 1L
for (code in names(scenario_vectors)) {
  for (dimension in dimensions) {
    for (factor in seq_len(dimension)) {
      eta_value <- scenario_vectors[[code]]$eta[[factor]]
      zeta_value <- scenario_vectors[[code]]$zeta[[factor]]
      discriminant <- zeta_value^2 + 4 * eta_value
      root_values <- (
        zeta_value + c(-1, 1) * sqrt(as.complex(discriminant))
      ) / 2
      max_real_root <- max(Re(root_values))
      regime <- if (eta_value < 0 && zeta_value < 0) {
        if (discriminant < 0) "Stable oscillatory" else "Stable nonoscillatory"
      } else if (max_real_root > 0) {
        if (discriminant < 0) "Anti-damped oscillatory" else "Amplifying nonoscillatory"
      } else {
        "Marginal or mixed"
      }

      stability_rows[[stability_row]] <- data.frame(
        Code = code,
        Dimensions = paste0(dimension, "D"),
        Factor = factor,
        eta = eta_value,
        zeta = zeta_value,
        Discriminant = discriminant,
        `Max Re(root)` = max_real_root,
        `rho(Phi[.4])` = exp(0.4 * max_real_root),
        `rho(Phi[.25])` = exp(0.25 * max_real_root),
        `g(H[100])` = exp((100 - 1) * 0.4 * max_real_root),
        `g(H[300])` = exp((300 - 1) * 0.25 * max_real_root),
        Regime = regime,
        check.names = FALSE
      )
      stability_row <- stability_row + 1L
    }
  }
}
stability_table <- dplyr::bind_rows(stability_rows) |>
  dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 4)))

cat("\\begingroup\\tiny\\setlength{\\tabcolsep}{2pt}\n")
print(knitr::kable(
  stability_table,
  format = "latex",
  longtable = TRUE,
  caption = "Deterministic stability diagnostics and modal exponential-rate factors g(H) = exp{H max Re(root)} for every reported scenario factor. The g(H) columns are modal-rate factors over the observed horizon, not total finite-horizon state amplification. H[100] = 39.6 and H[300] = 74.75 under the retained time-step rules.",
  booktabs = TRUE,
  escape = FALSE,
  align = c("c", "c", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r", "l")
))
cat("\\endgroup\n")
```
